issue.title: Make transfer execution viable for serverless deployment
issue.body:
## Goal

Follow up #20 / PR #22 by implementing and validating an execution strategy that is actually viable for the target serverless deployment.

#20 established that the current row-oriented executor is a correctness baseline, not an acceptable production shape for the target workload. At 10,000 source rows × 3 Destination Links it produced approximately:

- 150,012 serial DB calls for all no-op
- 180,012 serial DB calls for initial Black
- 360,012 serial DB calls for full immutable Red + Black

The follow-up goal is to reduce this request amplification while preserving the current transfer semantics and while balancing serverless duration/memory cost against shared PostgreSQL pressure.

## Ownership

**Implementation approach is AI-owned.**

Do not treat metadata batching, TEMP TABLE, CTE, memory JSON batching, bulk stored SQL, or any other mechanism as mandatory. PR #22 identifies bounded batching of Velvet-owned metadata SQL as the first low-risk experiment, but Astra may change course if measurements show another approach is simpler or more appropriate.

The important requirement is the resulting behavior and deployment fitness, not a prescribed architecture.

## Required semantics to preserve

Do not weaken existing Phase 1–5 and #19 behavior in order to improve throughput.

At minimum preserve:

- one complete source evaluation / fixed source snapshot per Run
- Dirty Key × Destination Link independent decision behavior
- immutable / mutable / insert_only semantics
- configured comparison exclusions
- exact returned-key validation
- duplicate handling/history
- Destination Link execution order where observable
- single atomic work transaction
- downstream failure rollback
- separately durable failed Run contract
- lost-COMMIT-response behavior
- #19 asymmetric no-op and correlated multi-destination behavior

## Serverless / deployment evaluation

The application is expected to run in a serverless environment where both execution duration and allocated memory affect cost. PostgreSQL is a shared resource, so moving work into the database is not automatically better.

Evaluate candidates using both sides of the system.

### Application side

- total invocation duration
- DB call count and serialized waiting
- peak RSS / heap / external memory
- source snapshot and intermediate/batch memory
- JSON/parameter serialization and GC behavior
- realistic app-to-DB RTT / network placement
- repeated runs and tail duration where practical

### PostgreSQL side

- DB CPU
- buffer/cache behavior
- I/O / WAL
- temp relation / sort / hash spill where relevant
- lock hold/wait time
- work-transaction duration
- connection occupancy
- aggregate throughput
- impact on representative unrelated DB work
- concurrent independent Settings

Do not invent provider-specific price thresholds if deployment budgets are not yet defined. Record assumptions and use comparative evidence.

## Timeout and backlog recovery risk

Serverless execution has a finite invocation lifetime. A design that only works when one Run can continue indefinitely is not viable.

For example, a standard AWS Lambda function currently has a maximum invocation timeout of 900 seconds / 15 minutes. Provider-specific or durable/asynchronous execution models may allow different limits, but Velvet must not assume an unbounded execution window.

This becomes more serious during an outage or downstream failure:

- transfer work / Dirty Keys / invocations may continue to accumulate while processing is unavailable or repeatedly fails
- after recovery, the system may face a backlog far larger than the ordinary steady-state workload
- attempting to drain that backlog can sharply increase serverless concurrency, DB connections, PostgreSQL CPU/I/O/locks, and downstream load
- that recovery load can trigger a second failure even though the original dependency has recovered
- if backlog arrival continues faster than the sustainable catch-up rate, or each recovery attempt times out before meaningful progress is made, the system can enter a state where it never catches up
- repeated timeout/retry/backlog growth can therefore turn a temporary outage into a practically unrecoverable condition

Treat this as a deployment/recoverability requirement, not merely a performance benchmark.

The implementation approach is deliberately unspecified. Do not assume any particular limiting, chunking, scheduling, throttling, queueing, or concurrency-control mechanism from this Issue. Astra should choose the smallest appropriate design after measuring the actual execution and recovery characteristics.

At minimum evaluate:

- maximum realistic work that can complete within the target runtime timeout with safety margin
- steady-state arrival rate versus sustainable processing throughput
- backlog growth for representative outage durations
- catch-up throughput after recovery while new work continues to arrive
- whether recovery traffic materially harms unrelated Settings, PostgreSQL, or downstream systems
- whether retries/timeouts create positive feedback that increases backlog faster than it is drained
- whether a finite backlog can be reduced to normal operating levels without weakening atomicity, history, or correctness

If target timeout/recovery behavior is not demonstrated, production adoption remains unresolved even if the normal steady-state benchmark is fast.

## Call amplification must remain visible

A partial optimization is acceptable as an experiment but not automatically sufficient for production.

For example, PR #22 notes that batching only Active / Work Item / Processing can still leave approximately 60,000 reassessment/comparison calls at 10,000 × 3, and even batching the fixed comparison can leave roughly 30,000 row-sized stored reassessment calls.

Therefore:

- measure residual serial calls after each experiment
- do not declare success merely because one metadata category was batched
- if residual calls remain outside the deployment envelope, continue to a more explicit bulk I/O/materialization design
- row-sized stored SQL may remain a throughput floor and must be evaluated rather than hidden

## Sequence / allocation

#20 also demonstrated that source evaluation can consume allocation/sequence candidates even for no-op rows, while a deferred-allocation kernel avoided most unused candidates.

Do not automatically rewrite arbitrary source SQL or extract `nextval(...)` expressions.

If post-decision allocation is pursued, require an explicit reviewable contract that preserves:

- stable business correlation
- per-link no-op independence
- exact key validation
- one source evaluation
- understandable failure/debug behavior

Sequence gaps themselves are not a business correctness problem.

## SQL reviewability / runtime construction

Keep SQL construction reviewable.

- minimize runtime-only SQL structure transformation
- prefer fixed/inspectable SQL and explicit bulk inputs where practical
- do not infer relation/identifier/predicate rewrites from arbitrary stored SQL
- run Serene and document ordinary / review-required / violation classifications for changed execution paths
- explain any SQL execution path outside the normal `src` audit scope and how it is reviewed
- do not suppress review-required findings merely to obtain a clean gate

## Operational oracles

The implementation/review should also consider issues surfaced during #20:

### Incident investigation

Make failures reasonably diagnosable. Ideally a failed execution can identify or reconstruct:

- Run / Setting
- Destination Link
- operation phase
- durable vs rolled-back state
- pending Dirty Keys / retryability
- executed SQL/configuration definition or version

Do not require a new logging framework unless justified; choose the smallest useful mechanism.

### Failure isolation

A failure or expensive Run for one Setting should not introduce an unnecessary global failure domain for unrelated Settings. Core semantics must not depend on a global mutex/stop condition. Shared DB saturation and host-level scheduling still need measurement rather than assumption.

### Registration / maintainability

Keep configuration and source definitions easy to inspect and debug.

- source SQL should remain independently executable/inspectable where possible
- avoid introducing registration-time side effects merely for optimization
- remember that a SELECT containing `nextval` or side-effecting functions is not inherently side-effect-free
- configuration changes should remain reviewable

## Suggested experiment progression — not mandatory

PR #22 recommends starting with bounded batching of Velvet-owned metadata SQL because it can attack measured request amplification without changing arbitrary stored SQL contracts.

That is a reasonable first experiment, not a required final design.

If residual calls, application memory, shared-DB pressure, timeout behavior, or backlog recovery remain unacceptable, Astra should continue evaluating alternatives under the same semantics and load rather than declare the partial optimization production-ready.

## Acceptance criteria

- current row-oriented executor remains available as correctness/reference evidence during development
- a candidate reduces measured DB-call amplification materially for 1,000 / 10,000 rows and 1 / 3 links
- all-no-op, mostly-no-op, initial Black and correction routes are included
- application duration/memory and shared PostgreSQL cost are both evaluated
- realistic/simulated RTT and at least representative concurrency effects are considered
- target runtime timeout and safety margin are explicitly considered
- steady-state and post-outage backlog/catch-up behavior are evaluated separately
- recovery from a representative finite backlog does not become an unresolved cascading-failure/repeated-timeout condition
- residual row-sized calls are explicitly reported
- Phase 1–5 + #19 behavior and rollback/failure contracts remain passing
- SQL construction/review path remains explicit and Serene findings are reported rather than hidden
- if the candidate is still not suitable for target deployment, say so and leave adoption unresolved instead of weakening correctness
- Fresh Alder review finds no unintended business-meaning change

## References

- #20 execution-strategy evaluation
- PR #22 measurement/Decision 0009
- #19 / PR #21 multi-destination correctness baseline

## Deliverable

- dedicated branch
- implementation/PoC with measurements against the current baseline
- Decision/update explaining chosen approach, evidence, limits and remaining risks
- review-ready PR
- do not merge automatically
